summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

primary_citations.citation_text: New Mexico - NMSA 1978 Chapter 32A, Article 4 (Abuse and Neglect Act: 32A-4-3 duty to report, 32A-4-18 custody hearings, 32A-4-19 adjudicatory hearings), CYFD-published Children's Code compilation (2023 text; 32A-4-3 amended 2025 by SB 42)

New Mexico Statutes Chapter 27 - Public Assistance (public assistance and Medicaid programs; CYFD's child-welfare authority is not in this chapter — it is the Children, Youth and Families Department Act, NMSA 1978 § 9-2A-7(D), and the Children's Code, NMSA 1978 § 32A-1-1, per 8.10.3.3 NMAC)

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Yvonne L. v. New Mexico Department of Human Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that children in New Mexico state custody had a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment right to reasonable safety measured by the Youngberg professional judgment standard and reversed qualified immunity on that claim, while affirming that 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(10) of the AACWA is too vague and amorphous to be enforced under Section 1983.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling circuit authority, arising from New Mexico, on the State's duty once it places a child in substitute care.
key_cases.quote: while it does not require actual knowledge the children will be harmed, it implies abdication of the duty to act professionally in making the placements

key_cases.case_name: M.D.R. v. State ex rel. Human Services Department
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal on sovereign immunity grounds, holding that the Tort Claims Act does not waive the State's immunity for the department's foster placement and supervision of children because placing a child in a foster home is neither the provision of 'health care services' under Section 41-4-10 nor the operation of a hospital or 'like facility' under Section 41-4-9.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing New Mexico decision on how far the State may be held answerable in tort for the foster placements it makes and supervises.
key_cases.quote: While the complaint alleges deplorable conduct by the Department, the Act does not waive the State's immunity from tort liability under the circumstances of this case

key_cases.case_name: Quevedo ex rel. Bevan v. New Mexico Children, Youth & Families Department
key_cases.holding: The court held that disputed material facts about whether and how CYFD placed children at a private residential ranch precluded summary judgment on whether the Tort Claims Act building waiver in Section 41-4-6(A) permitted suit, and it reversed and remanded.
key_cases.relevance: It concerns CYFD's responsibility for children it places in a privately operated congregate facility.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that questions of material fact preclude summary judgment on the issue of whether the TCA's building waiver applies to permit Plaintiffs' suit

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who failed to investigate abuse referrals and closed a foster child's case before he was starved and beaten to death were not entitled to qualified immunity, because the special relationship with a child in state custody and his right to reasonable safety were clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that the state's custodial duty continues for the whole duration of the placement, not just at the moment of placement.
key_cases.quote: plaintiffs sufficiently pled facts, when taken as true, that show Booker and Peagler plausibly violated Chandler's substantive due process right to be reasonably safe while in foster care

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a caseworker who recommended and maintained a child's placement with a father she had reason to believe was abusing him, and who withheld her concerns from the juvenile court, violated the child's clearly established substantive due process right to be free from state-created danger.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the caseworker's affirmative duties when recommending and continuing a placement for a child in state custody.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that, under Currier, Ms. Patton violated T.D.'s clearly established substantive due process constitutional right to be free of a state official's creation of danger from a private actor

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Mercer-Smith
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the purpose for which the district court exercised its contempt power against CYFD was not remedial and therefore could not be sustained as civil contempt, and it reversed the contempt order and vacated the nearly four-million-dollar award in its entirety.
key_cases.relevance: The underlying dispute was CYFD's foster placement of the children with former group-home employees in violation of the court's placement order.
key_cases.quote: we reverse the contempt order and vacate the award in its entirety
